Puṇḍarīka denotes the blossom of the lotus in the Rigveda and later. The pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa states that the lotus flower is born of the light of the Nakṣatras, and the Atharvaveda compares the human heart to the lotus.
Foot notes x. 142, 8.
taittirīya brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 2, 1; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 5, 6; Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad, ii. 3, 10; vi. 3, 14; Chāndogya Upaṇiṣad, i. 6, 7; aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 4.
xviii. 9, 6.
x. 8, 43; Chāndogya upaniṣad, viii. 1, 1.
In the taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 18, 1; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 2, 1, puṇḍari-srajā denotes a ‘wreath of lotus leaves.’
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 71.

Puṇḍra is the name of a people regarded as outcasts in the aitareya brāhmaṇa. Their name occurs in the Sūtras also. In the Epic their country corresponds with Bengal and Bihar.
Foot notes vii. 18; śāṅkhāyana śrauta sūtra, xv. 26.
baudhāyana dharma sūtra, i. 2, 14, Cf. Caland, Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft, 56, 553; Būhler, Sacred Books of the East, 14, 148; Oldenberg, Buddha, 394, n. For the later geographical position of the Puṇḍras, cf. the map in Pargiter, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1908, 333.
